claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths by 2030.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths by 2030 (Rahib et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rahib et al., 2014

claim: PDA has a 5-year survival rate of less than 10%.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths by 2030 (Rahib et al., 2014), and has a 5-year survival rate of <10%.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: Activating mutations in KRAS occur in approximately 95% of PDA cases.
source: The most common genetic alterations include activating mutations in KRAS in ~95% of PDA and inactivating mutations or deletions of TP53, CDKN2A, and SMAD4 in 50–70% (Jones et al., 2008; Biankin et al., 2012; Ryan et al., 2014; Waddell et al., 2015; Witkiewicz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to genomic studies

claim: Inactivating mutations or deletions of TP53, CDKN2A, and SMAD4 occur in 50-70% of PDA cases.
source: The most common genetic alterations include activating mutations in KRAS in ~95% of PDA and inactivating mutations or deletions of TP53, CDKN2A, and SMAD4 in 50–70% (Jones et al., 2008; Biankin et al., 2012; Ryan et al., 2014; Waddell et al., 2015; Witkiewicz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to genomic studies

claim: Transcriptional profiling has identified two main PDA subtypes termed classical and basal-like.
source: Recently, transcriptional profiling from resected PDA specimens has identified two main subtypes with distinct molecular features, termed classical and basal-like (Collisson et al., 2011; Moffitt et al., 2015; Bailey et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to three independent transcriptional profiling studies

claim: Classical PDA is enriched for expression of epithelial differentiation genes.
source: Classical PDA is enriched for expression of epithelial differentiation genes, whereas basal-like PDA is characterized by laminin and basal keratin gene expression, stem cell and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) markers, analogous to the basal subtypes previously defined in bladder and breast cancers (Perou et al., 2000; Parker et al., 2009; Curtis et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Damrauer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to subtype classification studies

claim: Basal-like PDA is characterized by laminin and basal keratin gene expression, stem cell and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) markers.
source: Classical PDA is enriched for expression of epithelial differentiation genes, whereas basal-like PDA is characterized by laminin and basal keratin gene expression, stem cell and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) markers, analogous to the basal subtypes previously defined in bladder and breast cancers (Perou et al., 2000; Parker et al., 2009; Curtis et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Damrauer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to subtype classification studies

claim: Basal-like subtype tumors display poorly differentiated histological features and correlate with markedly worse prognosis.
source: Importantly, basal-like subtype tumors display poorly differentiated histological features and correlate with markedly worse prognosis (Moffitt et al., 2015; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Aung et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical outcome studies

claim: PDA subtypes are preserved in organoids, cell line cultures, and genetically engineered mouse models.
source: These subtypes are preserved in different experimental models of PDA including organoids (Boj et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2015; Seino et al., 2018), cell line cultures (Collisson et al., 2011; Moffitt et al., 2015; Martinelli et al., 2017), and a genetically engineered mouse (GEM) model of PDA in which ablation of oncogenic Kras resulted in subtype conversion (Kapoor et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies using different model systems

claim: The Hedgehog pathway is activated in PDA.
source: The Hedgehog (Hh) pathway is activated in PDA and has been found to play important and complex roles in PDA pathogenesis (Morris et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Morris et al., 2010

claim: The developing and normal adult pancreas lack expression of Hh pathway ligands.
source: Whereas the developing and normal adult pancreas lack expression of Hh pathway ligands, the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) and Indian Hedgehog (IHH) ligands are prominently induced in the pancreatic epithelium upon injury and throughout PDA development, from early precursor pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) to invasive disease (Berman et al., 2003; Thayer et al., 2003; Prasad et al., 2005; Nolan-Stevaux et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of Hh ligand expression

claim: SHH and IHH ligands are prominently induced in the pancreatic epithelium upon injury and throughout PDA development from PanIN to invasive disease.
source: Whereas the developing and normal adult pancreas lack expression of Hh pathway ligands, the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) and Indian Hedgehog (IHH) ligands are prominently induced in the pancreatic epithelium upon injury and throughout PDA development, from early precursor pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) to invasive disease (Berman et al., 2003; Thayer et al., 2003; Prasad et al., 2005; Nolan-Stevaux et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies tracking Hh ligand expression during PDA progression

claim: Smo deletion in the pancreatic epithelium has no effect on mutant KRAS-driven PDA in GEM models.
source: While Smo deletion in the pancreatic epithelium has no effect on mutant KRAS-driven PDA in GEM models, studies from our group and others reveal a surprising role for SHH in restraining cancer growth (Lee et al., 2014; Mathew et al., 2014; Rhim et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to genetic studies in mouse models

claim: SHH has a role in restraining cancer growth in PDA.
source: While Smo deletion in the pancreatic epithelium has no effect on mutant KRAS-driven PDA in GEM models, studies from our group and others reveal a surprising role for SHH in restraining cancer growth (Lee et al., 2014; Mathew et al., 2014; Rhim et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies including authors' own work

claim: Activation of GLI transcription factors in the pancreatic epithelium is required for oncogenesis in PDA.
source: By contrast, several lines of evidence indicate that activation of GLI transcription factors in the pancreatic epithelium is required for oncogenesis in PDA (Dennler et al., 2007; Ji et al., 2007; Nolan-Stevaux et al., 2009; Rajurkar et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies of GLI function

claim: Pancreas-specific transgenic over-expression of the Gli3 repressor attenuates PDA progression.
source: First, pancreas-specific transgenic over-expression of the Gli3 repressor attenuates PDA progression (Rajurkar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rajurkar et al., 2012

claim: Forced Gli2 over-expression cooperates with oncogenic Kras to promote aggressive poorly differentiated tumors.
source: Second, forced Gli2 over-expression cooperates with oncogenic Kras to promote aggressive poorly differentiated tumors (Pasca di Magliano et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pasca di Magliano et al., 2006

claim: All PDA cell lines in the panel expressed Hh pathway proteins to varying degrees.
source: We found that all PDA cell lines expressed Hh pathway proteins to varying degrees.
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: GLI2 was readily detectable in 10 out of 14 PDA cell lines.
source: GLI1 and GLI3 expression were restricted to two- and one-cell line respectively, while GLI2 was readily detectable in 10/14 lines.
evidence: Based on immunoblot data in Figure 1A

claim: Cell lines expressing the highest levels of GLI2 displayed the lowest levels of SHH expression.
source: Notably, cell lines expressing the highest levels of GLI2 (KP4, MiaPaca and Panc0327 cells) displayed the lowest levels of SHH expression (Figure 1A; asterisk).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: GLI transcriptional activity was inversely correlated with SHH expression and positively correlated with GLI expression.
source: Accordingly, GLI responsive luciferase reporter assay (Sasaki et al., 1997) demonstrated that GLI transcriptional activity was inversely correlated with SHH expression and positively correlated with GLI expression (Figure 1B,C)
evidence: Based on luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1B,C

claim: All SHH-high cell lines lacked basal GLI reporter activity.
source: such that all SHHhi cell lines lacked basal reporter activity (Figure 1B)
evidence: Based on luciferase reporter data in Figure 1B

claim: GLI-high KP4, MiaPaca and Panc0327 lines exhibited the highest levels of GLI reporter activity.
source: whereas the GLIhi KP4, MiaPaca and Panc0327 lines exhibited the highest levels of activity (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Based on luciferase reporter data in Figure 1B,C

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of GLI2 suppressed GLI-driven luciferase activity.
source: Luciferase activity was specific to GLI proteins as shRNA-mediated knockdown of GLI2 or treating cells with GANT61 inhibitor, which blocks GLI binding to DNA (Lauth et al., 2007), suppressed GLI-driven luciferase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: Treatment with GANT61 inhibitor suppressed GLI-driven luciferase activity.
source: Luciferase activity was specific to GLI proteins as shRNA-mediated knockdown of GLI2 or treating cells with GANT61 inhibitor, which blocks GLI binding to DNA (Lauth et al., 2007), suppressed GLI-driven luciferase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D and citation to Lauth et al., 2007

claim: Tumors expressing high levels of GLI2 mRNA had significantly lower expression of SHH and IHH in TCGA samples.
source: Consistent with the cell line data, tumors expressing high levels of GLI2 mRNA had significantly lower expression of SHH and IHH (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on analysis of TCGA RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: High GLI2 status was independent of stromal cell content in TCGA PDA samples.
source: Importantly, given that stromal cells also express GLI2, we confirmed that high GLI2 status was independent of stromal cell content. Of the 51 PDA tumors characterized as GLI2 high, a relatively even distribution between high purity (>33% tumor/stromal cell content; n = 23) and low purity (<33% tumor/stromal cell content; n = 27) samples was observed (see Materials and methods for details), indicating that GLI2 expression in stromal cells is an unlikely confounding factor in determining tumor cell GLI2 status in this patient cohort.
evidence: Based on analysis of tumor purity data from TCGA samples

claim: High expression levels of GLI2 in primary PDA tumors correlated with shortened overall and disease-free survival.
source: Notably, high expression levels of GLI2 in primary PDA tumors correlated with shortened overall and disease-free survival (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: High SHH expression levels were associated with longer disease-free survival.
source: In contrast, high SHH expression levels were associated with longer disease-free survival (Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: GLI2 or SHH high versus low expression level was not correlated with clinical variables such as sex, T stage, N stage, or M stage.
source: GLI2 or SHH high versus low expression level was not correlated with clinical variables such as sex, T stage, N stage, or M stage, although as expected from our data there was a correlation between high SHH and low GLI2 expression and vice-versa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of clinical variables shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G

claim: Most GLI-high/Hh-low cell lines were in the EMT high group.
source: Notably, whereas none of the GLIlo/Hhhi cell lines showed an EMT signature, most of the GLIhi/Hhlo cell lines were in the EMT high group, with the exceptions, HupT3 and Panc0327, displaying an intermediate phenotype (Figure 2A; Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Based on immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 1B,C

claim: GLI activity correlated positively with EMT in the PDA cell line panel.
source: This signature assigned 38 human PDA cell lines as EMT high or low (Gröger et al., 2012; Viswanathan et al., 2017), and we found that GLI activity (see Figure 1B) correlated positively with EMT in our PDA cell line panel (Figure 2B)
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B using published EMT scores

claim: SHH expression correlated negatively with EMT.
source: and we found that GLI activity (see Figure 1B) correlated positively with EMT in our PDA cell line panel (Figure 2B), while SHH expression correlated negatively (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: PDA cell lines with elevated levels of epithelial marker expression closely correlated with enrichment of the classical gene program.
source: As expected, PDA cell lines with elevated levels of epithelial marker expression (GLIlo/Hhhi lines) closely correlated with enrichment of the classical gene program (Collisson et al., 2011; Aung et al., 2018) (Figure 2A and Figure 2D).
evidence: Based on gene expression data shown in Figure 2A and 2D

claim: GLI2 mRNA expression was enriched in basal-like tumors in TCGA samples.
source: Strikingly, GLI2 mRNA expression was enriched in the basal-like tumors, (Figure 2E left)
evidence: Based on analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 2E

claim: High SHH and IHH expression correlated with the classical subtype in TCGA samples.
source: whereas high SHH and IHH expression correlated with the classical subtype (Figure 2E middle, right).
evidence: Based on analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 2E

claim: GLI2 overexpression strongly induced mesenchymal markers ZEB1, VIM and basal-like marker KRT14 in YAPC cells.
source: Strikingly, GLI2 overexpression strongly induced the mesenchymal markers ZEB1, VIM and basal-like marker KRT14 in YAPC cells and led to downregulation of epithelial markers E-Cadherin and ESRP1, and the transcription factor GATA6 - a putative regulator of the classical subtype of PDA (Collisson et al., 2011; Martinelli et al., 2017) and SHH in YAPC and HPAFII cells (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A

claim: GLI2 overexpression led to downregulation of epithelial markers E-Cadherin and ESRP1, and the transcription factor GATA6 and SHH in YAPC and HPAFII cells.
source: Strikingly, GLI2 overexpression strongly induced the mesenchymal markers ZEB1, VIM and basal-like marker KRT14 in YAPC cells and led to downregulation of epithelial markers E-Cadherin and ESRP1, and the transcription factor GATA6 - a putative regulator of the classical subtype of PDA (Collisson et al., 2011; Martinelli et al., 2017) and SHH in YAPC and HPAFII cells (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: YAPC- and HPAFII-GLI2 cells showed a significant change in cell morphology characterized by a more elongated, less compact morphology.
source: Consistent with a switch toward a mesenchymal-like cell state, YAPC- and HPAFII-GLI2 cells showed a significant change in cell morphology compared to control cells expressing empty vector (EV) (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), characterized by a more elongated, less compact morphology when grown as monolayer cultures or as 3D matrigel cultures (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on microscopy images shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis indicated that 'Epithelial_Mesenchymal_Transition' was the most statistically significant program activated by GLI2.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using the Cancer Hallmarks database indicated that 'Epithelial_Mesenchymal_Transition' was the most statistically significant program activated by GLI2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Dox treatment of iGLI2 cells for 3 days resulted in a significant increase in basal-like subtype genes and a corresponding decrease in a subset of classical genes in both YAPC- and HPAFII-iGLI2 cells.
source: In keeping with the relationship between EMT and the basal-like subtype, qPCR analysis indicated that Dox treatment of iGLI2 cells for 3 days resulted in a significant increase in basal-like subtype genes and a corresponding decrease in a subset of classical genes in both YAPC- and HPAFII-iGLI2 cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The expression levels of stemness associated markers SOX2 and CD44 increased upon GLI2 induction in YAPC cells.
source: In addition, the expression levels of stemness associated markers SOX2 and CD44 increased (Figure 3F)
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 3F

claim: SHH and GATA6 showed a significant decrease upon GLI2 induction and basal-like subtype switching in YAPC cells.
source: while SHH and GATA6 showed a significant decrease upon GLI2 induction and basal-like subtype switching in YAPC cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Forced expression of constitutively active GLI2 lacking the N-terminal repressor domain led to a decrease in SHH and GATA6 levels in YAPC cells.
source: Similarly, forced expression of a constitutively active GLI2 lacking the N-terminal repressor domain (Pasca di Magliano et al., 2006) (ΔN-GLI2) also lead to a decrease in SHH and GATA6 levels in YAPC cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: Loss of GLI2 led to a decrease in basal-like markers (KRT5, KRT14) and SOX2 and induction of epithelial markers in basal-like cell lines.
source: To test whether GLI proteins are not only sufficient but also necessary to sustain the basal-like phenotype, we suppressed GLI2 levels via siRNA or shRNA-mediated knockdown or CRISPR-Cas9 mediated knockout in basal-like cell lines, KP4 and Panc0327. Loss of GLI2 led to a decrease in basal-like markers (KRT5, KRT14) and SOX2 and induction of epithelial markers (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Expression of the basal-like signature and EMT-associated genes were significantly reduced following GLI2 knockdown in KP4 cells.
source: Accordingly, expression of the basal-like signature and EMT-associated genes were also significantly reduced following GLI2 knockdown (KP4) (Figure 4B,C) or knockout (Panc0327) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4B,C

claim: GLI2 knockout in KP4 and Panc0327 cells resulted in a clear switch towards a more epithelial like morphology in 2D monolayer culture.
source: Similarly, GLI2 knockout in KP4 and Panc0327 cells (GLI2KO) resulted in a clear switch towards a more epithelial like morphology in 2D monolayer culture (Figure 4D) and 3D matrigel growth (KP4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on microscopy images shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: GLI2 knockdown or knockout in KP4 and Panc0327 cells showed a prominent nuclear relocalization of ESRP1.
source: Moreover, immunofluorescence staining followingGLI2 knockdown or GLI2KO in KP4 and Panc0327 cells, respectively, showed a prominent nuclear relocalization of ESRP1 relative to Cas9 control cells, where ESRP1 was predominantly cytoplasmic (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: KP4 GLI2 knockout cells showed a modest difference in in vitro growth rate.
source: KP4 GLI2KO cells showed a modest difference in in vitro growth rate (Figure 4F)
evidence: Based on growth curve data shown in Figure 4F

claim: GLI2 knockout tumor xenografts displayed significantly reduced in vivo growth relative to Cas9 control tumors.
source: however, GLI2KO tumor xenografts displayed significantly reduced in vivo growth relative to Cas9 control tumors (Figure 4G).
evidence: Based on tumor growth measurements shown in Figure 4G

claim: Slow growing KP4 GLI2 knockout tumors displayed reduced expression of the basal-like marker S100A2 and increased expression of the classical marker GATA6.
source: Importantly, slow growing KP4 GLI2KO tumors displayed reduced expression of the basal-like marker S100A2 (Figure 4H, top row) and increased expression of the classical marker GATA6 (Figure 4H, bottom row)
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4H

claim: Removal of Dox from iKRAS cell culture media led to a 50% reduction in Kras mRNA expression within 24 hr and complete extinction by 72 hr.
source: In this system, removal of Dox from the culture media led to a 50% reduction in Kras mRNA expression within 24 hr and complete extinction by 72 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: A reciprocal increase in Gli2 and Gli1 expression was evident within 24 hr of Dox removal and persisted for at least 5 days in iKRAS cells.
source: Interestingly, a reciprocal increase in Gli2 and Gli1 expression was evident within 24 hr of Dox removal and persisted for at least 5 days (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: There was a corresponding up-regulation of Zeb1 and Vim mRNA and of basal-like subtype genes following Kras extinction in iKRAS cells.
source: Moreover, there was a corresponding up-regulation of Zeb1 and Vim mRNA and of basal-like subtype genes, consistent with induction of EMT and basal-like features (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS in YAPC and HPAFII cells led to a concomitant increase in GLI expression, EMT markers and basal-like subtype genes.
source: Similarly, shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS in the human PDA cell lines YAPC and HPAFII led to a concomitant increase in GLI expression, EMT markers (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and basal-like subtype genes (Figure 5E).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5D, 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E

claim: Treatment of iKRAS4 cells with the GLI inhibitor GANT61 suppressed basal-like gene induction in response to KRAS ablation.
source: Importantly, expression of the basal-like program was dependent on GLI2, as treatment of iKRAS4 cells with the GLI inhibitor, GANT61 (5 μM), suppressed basal-like gene induction in response to KRAS* ablation (Figure 5F).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5F

claim: In the presence of Dox (KRAS on), iKRAS-GLI2 cells had a growth advantage over control cells.
source: In the presence of Dox (KRAS* on), iKRAS-GLI2 cells had a growth advantage over control cells (Figure 5G, quantified in graph; '+Dox').
evidence: Based on colony formation assay shown in Figure 5G

claim: Upon Dox withdrawal (KRAS off), control cells failed to form colonies after 6 days while iKRAS-GLI2 cells were able to form colonies within the same time frame.
source: Upon Dox withdrawal (KRAS* off), control cells (iKRAS-EV) failed to form colonies after 6 days while iKRAS-GLI2 cells were able to form colonies within the same time frame (Figure 5G, quantified in graph; '- Dox'; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Based on colony formation assay shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: Ectopic GLI2 expression rescued growth of iKRAS cells by 2.5 fold following Dox withdrawal in 3D spheroid culture.
source: This phenotype was recapitulated in 3D spheroid culture, where ectopic GLI2 expression rescued growth of iKRAS cells by 2.5 fold following Dox withdrawal (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Based on spheroid culture data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D

claim: Human YAPC-GLI2 PDA cells were capable of sustained growth as 3D spheroids following shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS relative to YAPC-EV cells.
source: Similarly, human YAPC-GLI2 PDA cells were capable of sustained growth as 3D spheroids following shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS* relative to YAPC-EV cells (Figure 5H,I; Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Based on spheroid culture data shown in Figure 5H,I and Figure 5—figure supplement 2E

claim: GLI2 is upregulated in 6 out of 7 Escaper cell lines, including 4 out of 7 lacking YAP1 induction.
source: Strikingly, we find that GLI2 is upregulated in 6/7 Escaper cell lines, including 4/7 lacking YAP1 induction.
evidence: Based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 5J

claim: Loss of GLI2 did not have a significant effect on spheroid growth in the presence of Dox compared to shGFP control cells.
source: In the presence of Dox, loss of GLI2 did not have a significant effect on spheroid growth compared to shGFP control cells (Figure 5K top row, L; Figure 5—figure supplement 2G top row, H).
evidence: Based on spheroid culture data shown in Figure 5K,L and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G,H

claim: The eventual emergence of resistant colonies in the absence of Dox was suppressed in shGLI2 cells compared with shGFP control.
source: However, the eventual emergence of resistant colonies in the absence of Dox was suppressed in shGLI2 cells compared with shGFP control (Figure 5K bottom row, M arrowheads; Figure 5—figure supplement 2G, bottom row, arrowheads and I).
evidence: Based on spheroid culture data shown in Figure 5K,M and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G,I

claim: Among the most upregulated transcripts expressed in YAPC-iGLI2 cells following GLI2 induction were genes encoding secreted factors including SPP1 (Osteopontin), FGF19 and SPOCK2 and the basal-like gene S100A2.
source: Among the most upregulated transcripts expressed in YAPC-iGLI2 cells following GLI2 induction were genes encoding secreted factors including Secreted Phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) encoding Osteopontin (OPN), fibroblast growth factor 19 (FGF19) and SPOCK2 [SPARC (Osteonectin)] and the basal-like gene S100A2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Upregulation of secreted OPN was confirmed in YAPC-iGLI2 and HPAFII-iGLI2 cells 3 days post-induction of GLI2.
source: We confirmed upregulation of secreted OPN in YAPC-iGLI2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and in a second cell line, HPAFII-iGLI2 (Figure 6B,C) 3 days post-induction of GLI2.
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Ectopic expression of ΔN-GLI2 in YAPC cells led to an increase in SPP1 expression.
source: Similarly, ectopic expression of ΔN-GLI2 in YAPC cells also led to an increase in SPP1 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Chromatin immuno-precipitation of GLI2 showed binding to a GLI consensus element found upstream of the human SPP1 transcriptional start site.
source: Consistent with direct regulation of SPP1 transcription, chromatin immuno-precipitation of GLI2 showed binding to a GLI consensus element found upstream of the human SPP1 transcriptional start site (Figure 6D) (Kijewska et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on ChIP data shown in Figure 6D and citation to Kijewska et al., 2017

claim: Expression of SPP1 is significantly increased in YAPC cells during basal-like subtype switching in response to KRAS suppression.
source: Expression of SPP1 is significantly increased in YAPC cells during basal-like subtype switching in response to KRAS* suppression (Figure 6E)
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6E

claim: GLI2-high basal-like cell lines expressed the highest levels of SPP1 mRNA and OPN protein levels in addition to higher levels of OPN receptors, CD44 and integrin β3, as well as integrin α5.
source: Accordingly, we found that GLI2-high basal-like cell lines expressed the highest levels of SPP1 mRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) and OPN protein levels in addition to higher levels of OPN receptors, CD44 and integrin β3, as well as integrin α5 (Figure 6F) (Weber et al., 1996; Rangaswami et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2018), compared to classical subtype cells.
evidence: Based on qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Knockdown of GLI2 alone or in combination with GLI1 led to a significant decrease in SPP1 transcript and secreted protein.
source: Moreover, knockdown of GLI2 alone or in combination with GLI1 led to a significant decrease in SPP1 transcript (Figure 6G,H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) and secreted protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Based on qPCR and ELISA data shown in Figure 6G,H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E

claim: Exposure of Capan2 cells to recombinant OPN led to a significant increase in expression of basal-like genes, and a decrease in a subset of classical genes.
source: Exposure of Capan2 cells to recombinant OPN led to a significant increase in expression of basal-like genes, and a decrease in a subset of classical genes (Figure 6I).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6I

claim: A similar induction of basal-like genes was observed in YAPC cells treated with exogenous OPN.
source: A similar induction of basal-like genes was also observed in YAPC cells treated with exogenous OPN (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F

claim: shRNA-mediated GLI2 knockdown in Panc0327 cells led to a decrease in 13 basal-like genes, of which 12 were significantly rescued following co-treatment with recombinant OPN.
source: shRNA-mediated GLI2 knockdown in Panc0327 cells led to a decrease in 13 basal-like genes, of which 12 were significantly rescued following co-treatment with recombinant OPN (Figure 6J).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6J

claim: OPN-deleted KP4 cells displayed a decrease in basal-like marker KRT14 and a concomitant increase in classical-associated markers, E-cadherin and GATA6.
source: OPN-deleted KP4 cells displayed a decrease in basal-like markers KRT14 (Figure 7B) and a concomitant increase in classical-associated markers, E-cadherin and GATA6 (Figure 7B,C)
evidence: Based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 7B,C

claim: OPN-deleted KP4 cells showed a switch toward a more epithelial like morphology on monolayer culture.
source: along with a switch toward a more epithelial like morphology on monolayer culture (Figure 7D).
evidence: Based on microscopy images shown in Figure 7D

claim: SPP1 knockout cells did not show a significant growth defect in vitro relative to Cas9 controls cells.
source: Similar to GLI2KO cells, SPP1KO cells did not show a significant growth defect in vitro relative to Cas9 controls cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: Based on growth curve data shown in Figure 7E

claim: SPP1 knockout cells displayed a dramatic defect in growth as tumor xenografts in mice.
source: However, SPP1KO cells displayed a dramatic defect in growth as tumor xenografts in mice (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: Based on tumor growth measurements shown in Figure 7F,G

claim: SPP1 knockout cells were significantly impaired in their ability to form metastatic tumors in the lungs of recipient mice following tail vein injection.
source: Similarly, SPP1KO cells were significantly impaired in their ability to form metastatic tumors in the lungs of recipient mice following tail vein injection, whereas Cas9 control cells gave rise to widespread metastatic disease (Figure 7H,I).
evidence: Based on histology and quantification shown in Figure 7H,I

claim: The reduced overall tumor burden of mice injected with SPP1 knockout cells led to their prolonged survival relative to the control cohort.
source: Accordingly, the reduced overall tumor burden of mice injected with SPP1KO cells led to their prolonged survival relative to the control cohort (Figure 7J).
